extracted.intended_audience: literate public; essayists and satirists writing for the periodical press
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing moral/satirical periodical essays that engage the public without libel, using anecdotes and restraint. Focus on tone, evidence, and rhetorical devices appropriate to early-18th-century essayists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous innuendo that invites personalized readings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man who has a good Nose at an Innuendo, smells Treason and Sedition in the most innocent Words that can be put together, and never sees a Vice or Folly stigmatized, but finds out one or other of his Acquaintance pointed at by the Writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t rely on suggestive hints that readers with a suspicious temper will immediately map onto real people. Example/anti-pattern: a reader who annotated The Duty of Man with villagers' names turned a general moral book into a perceived personal libel. If your satire is too easily read as a personal attack it will produce quarrels and misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious to avoid giving offence—use restraint devices when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The SPECTATOR is very cautious of giving Offence, and has therefore put two Dashes into his Pudding ... he leaves a blank Space without so much as a Consonant to direct us ... a Chasm, that in my Opinion looks modest enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commenting on powerful or sensitive subjects, employ prudential devices (asterisks, dashes, blanks, omissions) or modest phrasing to signal restraint. This can protect the writer from accusations while still delivering the point. The device both softens direct charge and demonstrates the author's prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When speaking for the public good, declare your mind clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: I love to speak out and declare my Mind clearly, when I am talking for the Good of my Country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On matters of public importance, favor clarity and frankness over coyness or excessive circumlocution. Do not flatter or curry favor with ill men for the sake of advancement—forthright moral judgment is preferable when intended for public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim satire at vices in general rather than identifiable individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Book was writ against all the Sinners in England ... the satyrical Passages might be applied to several others of two or three neighbouring Villages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame critical or satirical remarks as indictments of general vice or types, not as pointed portraits of named persons. Generalization reduces the risk of creating libel and preserves the essay’s moral intent. Use composite characters or generalized examples rather than explicit identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate moral points with concrete anecdotes and vivid examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly uses short stories (e.g., the Pipe-table encounter, Will Funnell's drinking account, the musical landlord, the quacks' market tricks) to make and enliven moral observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lively, specific anecdotes and characters to make abstract moral claims persuasive and memorable. Small, comic incidents (coffee-house quarrels, tavern virtuosi, quack advertisements) serve as efficient evidence for larger claims about human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require credible evidence for extraordinary claims; avoid empty puffery
rubrics_metrics.description: I concluded, that had all these Advertisers arrived to that Skill they pretend to, they would have had no Need for so many Years successively to publish to the World the Place of their Abode ... most of the bills agree in one Expression, viz. that (with God's Blessing) they perform such and such Cures: This Expression is certainly very proper and emphatical, for that is all they have for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making claims (medical, practical, or rhetorical), provide concrete proof or reliable instances rather than relying on formulas, pious tags, or continual advertisement. Readers are skeptical of boastful claims without demonstrable evidence; persuasive writing should supply credible examples or witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery requires perseverance—mute showmanship in craft is not a substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: He had broke such Quantities of them [pipes], that he had almost broke himself, before he had brought this Piece of Musick to any tolerable Perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If showcasing an unusual skill or formal novelty, the writer/performer should show the result of persistent practice rather than merely boast. Craft and skill for their own sake should be grounded in honest labor; trivial feats of ambition (puns, stunts) are less worthy than substantive accomplishment.
